title: Party Planner Math
goal: Your kid plans a real party from start to finish: the guests, the budget, the food, the decorations and the timeline. The catch is $5 per guest, and every slice of pizza and every balloon has to fit inside it. Then they host it and work out what it really cost.
need: A reason to celebrate: a birthday, a new season, a family milestone, or just because
Paper, a pencil and a calculator
A budget of $5 per guest, real money if you can. For 8 guests, that's $40.
A kitchen for food prep and a space for the party: living room, backyard or park

lesson.text: When you divide food into packs, the answer is often a fraction. You can't buy half a bottle, so you round up, then check it still fits the budget.
lesson.before: 9 guests × 2 cups = 18 cups. A bottle holds 4 cups, so we need 4 bottles.

model.line: You can't buy half a bottle. 4 bottles leaves two guests with nothing, so buy 5.
5 bottles × $2 = $10. Does that fit the food budget?
Food rounds up. The budget decides what's on the menu.

lesson.modelNote: That's the maths at every step of this guide: multiply by the guests, divide into packs, round up, then check it fits.

howTo.intro: You don't need teaching experience. You're the party advisor, not the planner. Let them make the calls and run the numbers, and help only when they're stuck. You handle the knives, the oven and checking allergies with the guests' families.

plan.what: Pick the party, count the guests and split the budget (Steps 1 and 2).
Work out the food per guest and price it (Step 3).
Shop, prep and count back the timeline (Step 4).
Host it, then do the final maths (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Let the budget do the talking. 25 × $5 is $125, and they'll scale it down on their own once they price the food.
Don't fix it. Ask what could be homemade, borrowed or cut. Making that trade-off is the real lesson.

skills.name: Adapting
skills.text: when the plan changes on the day

steps.title: Pick the party and the guests
steps.why: The guest count sets everything else, starting with the budget.
steps.kid: Your kid decides what they're celebrating and picks a theme, a date and a time. Then they write the guest list and count the total, including family. Their budget is $5 per guest, so the headcount decides how much they have to spend.
steps.you: Help brainstorm if they're stuck, but let them choose. Ask 'do we have room for that many?' and remind them a small party counts. A backyard picnic for 4 is a real party.
ask: 8 guests at $5 each. What's your budget?
If you invite 4 more people, what changes?
steps.tip: Count yourself and your family in the headcount. They eat too.

levels.explore: A family party for 3 to 5 people. Pick a theme and count the guests.
levels.develop: 8 to 12 guests, with a list of yes, no and maybe, and the budget worked out.
levels.extend: Work out the smallest and largest headcount, and the budget for each.

steps.title: Split the budget
steps.why: Every dollar gets a job before anything gets bought.
steps.kid: Your kid splits the budget into food and drinks, decorations, activities and a little for surprises, and gives each one a dollar amount. For decorations they sort every idea into three piles: make it, already have it, buy it. Then they check the amounts add up to the total.
steps.you: Ask 'what matters most to spend on?' and 'what could you make or borrow instead?' Let them decide the split, even if you'd do it differently.
ask: You have $40 and food costs $32. How much is left?
Which decoration makes the biggest difference for the least money?
steps.tip: 8 guests: food $32, decorations $4, activities $0 (games you own), surprises $4. Check: 32 + 4 + 0 + 4 = $40.

levels.explore: Split the budget into 2 or 3 parts and write down each amount.
levels.develop: Use 4 categories, check they add up, and plan one free decoration.
levels.extend: Price every item in each category and work out the cost per guest for each one.

steps.title: Work out the food per guest
steps.why: Multiply, divide, round up, then check the budget.
steps.kid: Your kid picks the food and drinks. For each one they multiply by the guests, divide by the pack size, round up and price it. Then they add it all up and check it fits the food budget.
steps.you: Before they plan, check with each guest's family about allergies and foods they can't eat, and pass that on. Then let them run the numbers.
ask: 8 guests × 2 slices. A pizza has 8 slices. How many pizzas?
You're $3 over the food budget. What do you swap or cut?
steps.tip: Plot twist, the day before shopping: 'Two more guests are coming, and the budget stays at $40.' Now it's 3 pizzas ($36) and 5 bottles ($10). Let them find the fix, like homemade pizza for about $22.

levels.explore: Choose 3 or 4 foods and work out how many of each you need.
levels.develop: Plan the whole menu, work out amounts and prices, and check the food budget.
levels.extend: Handle the plot twist and plan a backup if something is too expensive or sold out.

steps.title: Shop and count back the timeline
steps.why: Real prices, and a plan for party day that starts at the end.
steps.kid: Your kid shops from their list and writes down the real price next to each guess. Then they build the party-day schedule by counting back from when guests arrive: setup time, food out, last check, plus a buffer in case something runs late.
steps.you: Let them lead the shopping and prep. Help with knives and the oven, not with decisions. Ask 'how long will setup really take?'
ask: Setup takes 90 minutes and the party starts at 2:00. When do you start?
Was anything cheaper or more expensive than you guessed?
steps.tip: 2:00 minus 90 minutes is 12:30. Add a 15-minute buffer and start at 12:15.

levels.explore: Gather what you need and write a timeline with 5 time slots.
levels.develop: Record real prices vs guesses and write an hour-by-hour plan with a buffer.
levels.extend: Keep a running total while shopping, and plan for 2 things that could go wrong on the day.

steps.title: Host it and do the final maths
steps.why: The party is the test, and the numbers are the report.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up from their plan and hosts: welcomes guests, serves the food, runs the games and handles small surprises. After, before anything is thrown out, they count what's left. Then they add up the receipts, compare with the budget and work out the cost per guest.
steps.you: Help with heavy things during setup, then let them be the host. When the juice runs low or a game flops, wait before you help.
ask: If you had $5 less, what would you cut?
steps.tip: Spent $35.90 of $40, so $4.10 under. Per guest: $35.90 ÷ 8 = about $4.49. 16 slices, 3 left, 13 eaten: 2 pizzas was right.

levels.explore: Host the party, then add up what you spent. Over or under?
levels.develop: Compare planned vs real costs, and work out the cost per guest.
levels.extend: Write a party report: budget vs real, leftovers, and what you'd change next time.

reference.title: Party Planner's Cheat Sheet
reference.intro: Ballpark amounts for a kids' party of about 2 hours. Every crowd is different, so count the leftovers and adjust next time.

after.label: Party formulas
lines: How many = guests × per guest ÷ pack size, rounded up
Cost per guest = total spent ÷ guests

conclusion.headline: They threw a real party.
conclusion.text: From the guest list to the last slice of pizza, your kid made the calls: how many people, how much food, what it would cost, and what to do when the plan changed. They multiplied, divided, rounded up, added receipts and worked to a clock. And they did it for people they care about.
conclusion.celebrate: Tell them what you noticed: the moment they figured out the juice wouldn't stretch, or how calmly they handled a guest who showed up early.
extensions: Plan for a bigger group and see how the budget and amounts scale
Plan a themed dinner with 3 courses and work out the cost per course
Compare a homemade party with a party at a venue for the same guests
Plan a surprise party, and keep it secret while working with others

signs: They ask 'how many people?' before 'how much food?'
They round up when they divide food into packs
They count back from a start time to plan their day
makeItReal: For the next birthday or family dinner, hand them the headcount and the budget. The planning is theirs, and so is the credit.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.caption: Italian night: every guest builds their own pizza.

fromHome.text: My daughter organized an Italian party where every guest made their own pizza. She worked out how much dough, sauce and cheese she needed per guest, wrote the shopping list and did the shopping. She made all the decorations herself, the flags, the garland and the ITALY sign, and even made Italian money so her friends could play restaurant.
